final.title: Table extraction is only the first step
final.body:
Table extraction is useful, but it is only the first step. If you pull line items into a sheet and stop there, you still have to decide what happens next: who checks the data, what rule sends it forward, and what gets recorded for later review. That is usually where the manual work lives.

For an owner-operator, the useful question is not “can we extract the table?” It is “which step after extraction repeats, follows a clear rule, and still eats my time?” If you cannot name that step, extraction alone may be enough. If you can, you may have a bounded workflow worth automating.

A practical example is a back-office flow where extracted data is checked for duplicates, compared against a simple amount rule, logged, and then handed back for human approval before any money moves. Human approval stays mandatory for high-risk decisions. In Bareni’s work, finished code is handed over and the customer’s database, automation-tool accounts, and API accounts are in the customer’s name from the start; that is working policy, not a warranty.

So the next step is simple: write down the step after extraction, the rule it follows, and the time it costs you each week. That tells you whether you need automation or just a better table.
